The Western blue groper (Achoerodus gouldii) attains a standard length at puberty of 65.3 cm [Lp = 65.3 cm], a metric that marks the transition from the growing juvenile phase into reproductive competence. Gravid females and mature males collected along the southern coastline of Australia show that this length is typically achieved after several years of benthic life on shallow reef habitats. The ultimate standard length for males reaches 116 cm [Li = 116 cm], a value derived from extensive field surveys of adult male specimens. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in maximum size is linked to the species' protogynous reproductive system, where larger, older males dominate spawning territories. Juveniles forage among macroalgae and seagrass beds, feeding predominantly on crustaceans and molluscs, and as they grow they shift toward larger, harder-shelled prey items. The species is endemic to temperate waters of southern Australia, where it is considered a long-lived, slow-growing labrid with high site fidelity. Growth rates decelerate markedly after the attainment of sexual maturity, a pattern consistent with many iteroparous reef fishes that allocate increasing resources to gonad development rather than somatic expansion. The ultimate standard length for females and smaller males, however, is approximately 90 cm [Li = approximately 90 cm], reflecting the size distribution in populations before sex change.

Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae of Achoerodus gouldii weigh just 0.00027 grams [Wwb = just 0.00027 grams] at the moment of eclosion, reflecting the modest diameter of the fertilised eggs, which measure approximately 0.8 mm in diameter. These minute, lecithotrophic prolarvae remain non-feeding for the first several days of life, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves while drifting in the pelagic environment. Under thermal conditions typical of the species' southern Australian spawning grounds, measured at 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], the age at birth, defined as the interval from egg fertilisation to chorion rupture, is approximately 9.5 days [ab = approximately 9.5 days]. This brief embryonic period is comparable to that of other temperate labrids with pelagic eggs. Following eclosion, the free-swimming larvae enter a pelagic larval phase that can last several weeks before metamorphosis and settlement. Mortality during this early planktonic stage is extremely high, a common feature among marine teleosts with broadcast spawning and small egg size. The tiny initial mass places an upper bound on the duration of yolk dependency, which in turn constrains the timing of first exogenous feeding.

Females of Achoerodus gouldii exhibit a maximum reproductive output that has been estimated from field studies of spawning aggregations along the lower west coast. At a stable water temperature of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], each mature female produces approximately 1,104 eggs daily [Ri = approximately 1,104 eggs daily] during the peak spawning season, a remarkable rate sustained over several months. This daily egg production, derived from counts of hydrated oocytes in gravid individuals, is among the highest recorded for any temperate labrid and reflects the substantial energetic investment females channel into gametogenesis. The eggs are pelagic and are released into the water column during serial spawning events, with individual females likely spawning on multiple consecutive days. Comparable fecundity estimates for congeneric species suggest that this high output is an adaptation to the intense predation pressure on pelagic eggs and larvae in coastal reef ecosystems. Diel periodicity in spawning has been observed, with peak activity occurring during late afternoon and early evening hours. The protracted spawning season, spanning the austral spring and summer, allows females to spread reproductive risk across the season and may enhance recruitment variability in response to fluctuating oceanographic conditions.

This translates to roughly 70 years, positioning Achoerodus gouldii as one of the longest-lived reef fishes in temperate Australia, a life-history strategy associated with slow somatic growth, late maturity, and low natural mortality among adults. The oldest documented individuals are consistently males, reflecting the protogynous sex-change pattern in which the largest, most dominant females transition to males after decades of reproductive activity. These extreme longevities are achieved at a water temperature of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], a relatively cool thermal regime that depresses metabolic rates compared to tropical labrids and likely contributes to reduced cellular senescence. The trade-off for such extended lifespan includes a delayed onset of reproductive activity: age at maturity for females is not reached until well over a decade. Seasonal growth increments in the otoliths become increasingly compressed after age 20, confirming the asymptotic approach toward ultimate body size.

This late onset of reproductive effort, recorded at a water temperature of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], is a direct consequence of the species' slow growth trajectory and the time required to reach the standard length at puberty of 65.3 cm [Lp = 65.3 cm]. Once mature, adult females grow slowly toward the ultimate wet weight, which attains approximately 20,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 20,000 grams] in the largest recorded individuals. Males, which arise through sex change from the largest females, can reach a comparable ultimate wet weight (20,000 grams) [Wwi = 20,000 grams], though their ultimate standard length of 116 cm [Li = 116 cm] reflects continued somatic growth after sex inversion. The combination of extreme longevity, late maturity, and high fecundity per spawning event characterises a conservative life-history strategy that makes the species vulnerable to overfishing, as removal of large, old individuals disproportionately impacts population reproductive output. Conservation measures including size limits and marine protected areas have been implemented across its range.
